A **ring system** is a disc or ring, orbiting an [astronomical object](Astronomical_object "Astronomical object"), that is composed of solid material such as [dust](Cosmic_dust "Cosmic dust") and [moonlets](Moonlet "Moonlet"), and is a common component of [satellite systems](Satellite_system_(astronomy) "Satellite system (astronomy)") around giant planets like <Saturn>. A ring system around a planet is also known as a **planetary ring** system.[[1]](Ring_system#cite_note-EA-20190312-1)

The most prominent and most famous planetary rings in the [Solar System](Solar_System "Solar System") are [those around Saturn](Rings_of_Saturn "Rings of Saturn"), but the other three [giant planets](Giant_planet "Giant planet") ([Jupiter](Rings_of_Jupiter "Rings of Jupiter"), [Uranus](Rings_of_Uranus "Rings of Uranus"), and [Neptune](Rings_of_Neptune "Rings of Neptune")) also have ring systems. There are also dust rings around the Sun at the distances of [Mercury](Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), <Venus>, and Earth, in [mean motion resonance](Mean_motion_resonance "Mean motion resonance") with these planets.[[1]](Ring_system#cite_note-EA-20190312-1)[[2]](Ring_system#cite_note-2)[[3]](Ring_system#cite_note-3) Recent evidence suggests that ring systems may also be found around other types of astronomical objects, including minor planets, moons, brown dwarfs, and other stars.

## Ring systems of planets

There are three ways that thicker planetary rings have been proposed to have formed: from material of the [protoplanetary disk](Protoplanetary_disk "Protoplanetary disk") that was within the [Roche limit](Roche_limit "Roche limit") of the planet and thus could not coalesce to form moons, from the debris of a [moon](Natural_satellite "Natural satellite") that was disrupted by a large impact, or from the debris of a moon that was disrupted by [tidal stresses](Tidal_stress "Tidal stress") when it passed within the planet's Roche limit. Most rings were thought to be unstable and to dissipate over the course of tens or hundreds of millions of years, but it now appears that Saturn's rings might be quite old, dating to the early days of the Solar System.[[4]](Ring_system#cite_note-4)

Fainter planetary rings can form as a result of meteoroid impacts with moons orbiting around the planet or, in case of Saturn's E-ring, the ejecta of cryovolcanic material.[[5]](Ring_system#cite_note-Spahn-5)[[6]](Ring_system#cite_note-Porco_Helfenstein_et_al._2006-6)

Sometimes rings will have ["**shepherd**" **moons**](Shepherd_moon "Shepherd moon"), small [moons](Natural_satellite "Natural satellite") that orbit near the inner or outer edges of rings or within gaps in the rings. The [gravity](Gravity "Gravity") of shepherd moons serves to maintain a sharply defined edge to the ring; material that drifts closer to the shepherd moon's orbit is either deflected back into the body of the ring, ejected from the system, or accreted onto the moon itself.

Jupiter's ring system was the third to be discovered, when it was first observed by the *Voyager 1* probe in 1979,[[9]](Ring_system#cite_note-:0-9) and was observed more thoroughly by the *Galileo* orbiter in the 1990s.[[10]](Ring_system#cite_note-10) Its four main parts are a faint thick torus known as the "halo"; a thin, relatively bright main ring; and two wide, faint "gossamer rings".[[11]](Ring_system#cite_note-11) The system consists mostly of dust.[[9]](Ring_system#cite_note-:0-9)[[12]](Ring_system#cite_note-12)

### Saturn

Main article: [Rings of Saturn](Rings_of_Saturn "Rings of Saturn")

Saturn's rings are the most extensive ring system of any planet in the Solar System, and thus have been known to exist for quite some time. [Galileo Galilei](Galileo_Galilei "Galileo Galilei") first observed them in 1610, but they were not accurately described as a disk around Saturn until [Christiaan Huygens](Christiaan_Huygens "Christiaan Huygens") did so in 1655.[[13]](Ring_system#cite_note-13) The rings are not a series of tiny ringlets as many think, but are more of a disk with varying density.[[14]](Ring_system#cite_note-14) They consist mostly of water ice and trace amounts of [rock](Rock_(geology) "Rock (geology)"), and the particles range in size from micrometers to meters.[[15]](Ring_system#cite_note-15)

content:
Based on my research, here's a comprehensive overview of which planets in our solar system have ring systems:

## Planets WITH Ring Systems:

### 1. **Jupiter** ✅
- Ring system discovered by Voyager 1 in 1979
- Consists of four main parts: a halo torus, a main ring, and two gossamer rings
- Made mostly of dust

### 2. **Saturn** ✅
- The most extensive and famous ring system
- Known since 1610 (Galileo Galilei), accurately described in 1655 (Christiaan Huygens)
- Consists mostly of water ice with trace amounts of rock
- Particles range from micrometers to meters in size

### 3. **Uranus** ✅
- Discovered in 1977 by James L. Elliot, Edward W. Dunham, and Jessica Mink
- Has 13 distinct rings identified
- Dark and opaque, only a few kilometers wide
- Likely consists of water ice and radiation-processed organics

### 4. **Neptune** ✅
- Conclusive discovery by Voyager 2 in 1989
- Five principal rings
- Faint and dusty, similar to Jupiter's rings
- 20-70% of the rings are dust
- Made of very dark organics processed by radiation

## Planets WITHOUT Ring Systems:

### 5. **Mercury** ❌ - No ring system

### 6. **Venus** ❌ - No ring system

### 7. **Earth** ❌ - No ring system
- (There are dust rings at Earth's distance from the Sun in mean motion resonance, but these aren't planetary rings)

### 8. **Mars** ❌ - No current ring system
- However, evidence suggests its moon Phobos will break up and form a ring in about 50 million years due to tidal deceleration

---

**Summary:** Out of the eight planets in our solar system, **four have ring systems** (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune) - all of these are gas/ice giants. The four **terrestrial planets** (Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars) do not have ring systems.
